config.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal

intro.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that performs a level order traversal on a binary tree, returning the node values grouped by their depth. You will learn the core concept of breadth-first search (BFS) using a queue data structure to process nodes layer by layer. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays for the queue and result storage, along with basic tree node objects. This beginner-friendly lesson will guide you step-by-step through the algorithm, helping you understand how to systematically explore hierarchical data.
intro.usecase: Level order traversal is essential for processing hierarchical data in breadth-first order, which appears in many real-world applications. For example, when displaying organizational charts in HR software, you need to show all employees at each management level before moving deeper into the hierarchy. This same pattern is used in file system explorers to show folders and files at each depth level, or in social networks to find connections within specific degrees of separation. Understanding this algorithm helps developers efficiently handle tree-structured data in user interfaces and backend processing.

objectives: Implement a queue data structure to manage nodes during traversal
Construct a function that performs breadth-first traversal of a binary tree
Initialize and manipulate arrays to store nodes at each level
Apply conditional logic to handle empty trees and edge cases
Integrate level tracking to separate nodes into distinct arrays
Render the traversal results as a nested array structure
Control the traversal loop to process all nodes in the correct order

content.body: Imagine you're a park ranger exploring a forest of trees. You want to map each level of branches systematically. In this lesson, we'll learn how to traverse a binary tree level by level, collecting all nodes at each depth. This is called Level Order Traversal.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain what level order traversal means for a binary tree.
2. Implement a queue-based approach to traverse levels.
3. Build a result array containing nodes grouped by level.
4. Handle edge cases like empty trees gracefully.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body:
Look at this simple binary tree. The root (3) is at level 0. Its children (9 and 20) are at level 1. Their children (15 and 7) are at level 2.

If we explore level by level, which order would we visit the nodes?
content.title: Explore the tree
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body: You likely started at the root, then moved to its children, then to their children. This natural top-down, left-to-right exploration is exactly level order traversal. You visited nodes level by level rather than diving deep down one branch first.
content.title: What you did

content.body: For a small tree, it's easy to track levels manually. But with hundreds of nodes, we need a systematic method to ensure we visit every node at the current level before moving deeper. How can we process nodes in this level-by-level fashion efficiently?
content.title: Why order matters

content.body: Think of exploring branches from a root. We start at the root, then explore all direct branches (children) before going deeper. This is like reading a book page by page, not jumping ahead. We'll use a queue to help us track which nodes to visit next, ensuring we handle one complete level before the next.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Use branch/root visual reasoning; visiting nodes or exploring levels one at a time.

content.body: We'll use a queue (First-In-First-Out) to process nodes. Start by enqueuing the root. While the queue isn't empty, process all nodes currently in the queue (one level), enqueue their children, and add the level's values to our result. This guarantees level-by-level traversal.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. If the tree is empty, return an empty array.
2. Initialize a queue with the root node.
3. While the queue has nodes:
   a. Record the current queue size (this is the level's node count).
   b. Create an array to store this level's values.
   c. For each node in the current level:
      i. Dequeue it and add its value to the level array.
      ii. Enqueue its left child if it exists.
      iii. Enqueue its right child if it exists.
   d. Add the level array to the result.
4. Return the result array of arrays.
